current_answer: Two studies of GitHub Copilot and hiring point in different directions. A 2026 NBER conference abstract estimates about 35% fewer technical-worker hires within a year among large firms induced to adopt by software-contract renewal, with no matching rise in separations. An April journal paper using LinkedIn and GitHub records associates adoption with a 3–5% higher monthly probability of hiring a software engineer, mainly at entry level. They count different outcomes in different firms; neither figure is a forecast for one worker or proof of an economy-wide job effect.

catalogue_card.question: Does Copilot cut software hiring?
catalogue_card.text: One conference estimate finds fewer technical hires after adoption; another study links adoption to a higher chance of any software-engineer hire. Different measures, no personal forecast.

summary: An NBER 2026 conference abstract estimates about 35% fewer technical hires among large firms induced to adopt GitHub Copilot by contract-renewal timing, without a rise in separations.
A separate April journal abstract associates adoption with a 3–5% higher monthly probability of a software-engineer hire, driven by entry-level hiring.
These are different samples and outcomes; the full studies were not accessible here, so a shared causal or economy-wide verdict is not justified.
uncertainty: The 35% estimate is available here only in an NBER conference abstract; the full paper, slides, precision and robustness checks were not accessible for this run.
The 3–5% result measures the probability that a firm hires a software engineer in a month, not the number of hires; its full article and proprietary data were not accessible.
Different samples, adoption definitions, hiring outcomes and research designs prevent treating the estimates as a direct replication or averaging them.
Neither study supplies an economy-wide effect, worker wages, or an individual job-risk probability.
